facts.statement: Zapsalis is classified as a genus of dromaeosaurine theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Zapsalis is a genus of dromaeosaurine theropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The genus Zapsalis was first described by the American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope in 1876.
facts.quote: Fossils of Zapsalis were first described by American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope in 1876

facts.statement: Cope named Zapsalis during the Bone Wars, a period of intense competition with paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: Cope named Zapsalis during the Bone Wars, his competition with Yale paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh

facts.statement: All known fossils of Zapsalis were collected from the Campanian age strata of the Judith River Formation in Montana, USA.
facts.quote: All of the fossils were collected from the Campanian age strata of the Judith River Formation in Montana, USA.

facts.statement: The type tooth of Zapsalis abradens is 12 mm long, flat on the inner side, lacks inner serrations, and has three outer serrations per millimeter.
facts.quote: The type tooth of Z. abradens is flat lingually, with no mesial serrations and 3 distal serrations per millimeter and is 12 mm in total length.

facts.statement: The type tooth of Zapsalis abradens features three inner ridges and four outer ridges.
facts.quote: There are three lingual ridges and four labial ones.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the second premaxillary teeth of Zapsalis may have been specialized for preening feathers.
facts.quote: The second premaxillary teeth of Zapsalis and other dromaeosaurids may have been structurally specialized for preening feathers, as seen in some Oviraptorosaurs as well.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Zapsalis is distinct from Saurornitholestes langstoni, as some researchers argue the Zapsalis teeth belong to S. langstoni while others maintain separation due to the indeterminate nature of the type species holotype.
facts.quote: In 2019, Currie and Evans announced that the Zapsalis teeth from the Dinosaur Park Formation represented the second premaxillary tooth of Saurornitholestes langstoni, in a paper describing a complete skull of that species. The authors kept the species distinct because the type species' holotype is likely indeterminate on a species level.

facts.statement: Zapsalis belongs to the family Dromaeosauridae.
Zapsalis lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 75 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 millones de años, en el Campaniense en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The type tooth of Zapsalis abradens is 1.2 cm long, flat on the inner side, lacks inner serrations, and has three outer serrations per millimeter.
facts.quote: El diente tipo de Z. abradens es plano lingualmente, sin dentado mesial y 3 dentados distales por milímetro y tiene 1,2 centímetros de longitud total.

facts.statement: The type tooth of Zapsalis abradens has three inner ridges and four outer ridges.
facts.quote: Hay tres crestas linguales y cuatro labiales.

facts.statement: The specific name abradens means "abrading" in Latin.
facts.quote: El nombre específico significa "abrasión" en latín.

facts.statement: The time range for Zapsalis is estimated from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian, between 85.7 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Maastrichtian (85.7 to 66 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Derek Larson and Philip Currie recognized Zapsalis as a valid taxon in 2013.
rejected.quote: It wasn't until 2013 Derek Larson and Philip Currie recognised Zapsalis as a valid taxon
